Grey Goo, an RTS released last year, gets a free expansion and permanent price reduction
How's the game going? Is it improving?

I'll admit to some bias here as I liked the game at launch.

They implemented servers for match stability, they did a comprehensive performance patch which doubled the frame rate I was seeing in the game, they've added replays, leagues (a la StarCraft: bronze, silver, gold etc) and player rating (e.g. this person was a tool or this person was a good opponent) observer mode... maybe I'm forgetting some stuff too.

They did a 3 mission mini campaign featuring what happened with Singleton in between their second and third acts of their original campaign, which i BELIEVE is included in the expansion content.

The expansion adds a new faction that is more micro-friendly than the original factions but I believe is pretty well balanced against them. Each original faction also gets a new unit that is a little more micro-friendly to increase the benefits of skillful play with units.

They increase the viability of economic harassment by making harvesters spawn less frequently and carry more resources (so killing them off is more valuable now) and re-balanced some of the faction's unique aspects (like the human teleporter)

Over all the game is a LOT better than it was when it launched last year. Fundamentally, it still plays pretty much the same so if you weren't interested in the fundamental gameplay you might not enjoy its current iteration, but a lot of things have improved a great deal since last year.

EDIT - if I had one wish about the game at this point, it's that the early game would be a bit quicker. Otherwise I'm happy with it

I am a huge fan of the game, but I try to be fair when telling others about it. Hope this helps :)

Also if you or anyone else is interested, I did a 2 part series on how Grey Goo stacks up against the classic C&C games, as one of its claims is that it's a throwback and is based partially on their model (GG has some devs that worked on the C&C games)

economy comparison: http://waywardstrategist.com/2015/07/01/is-grey-goo-an-homage-to-classic-rts-part-1-economy-and-basebuilding/

unit comparison: http://waywardstrategist.com/2015/07/08/is-grey-goo-an-homage-to-classic-rts-part-2-map-and-unit-design/

Played the game during a free weekend on Steam. Although it has an interesting setting, the gameplay really lacked the oomph to glue you to the game. I also had some issues with the general unit design (i.e. that one Beta unit that was literally useless unless you packed it into a wall turret, humans having to wire their first mining expansions to their main base, etc.).

That, and from what i've heard, the multiplayer community is more or less dead in the water due to several launch issues from which it never really recovered.

That Beta unit is called the Guardian, and I seldom see it in ranked play due to this drawback. However, many Beta do play with turret contains (mostly Predators on wall sections) which actually is devastatingly effective. I think the main reason you don't see Guardians more is they're relatively expensive and comparatively hard to tech to. They're also GREAT defensively, have AA ability and work well attached to the Hand of Ruk. Just because a unit is situational doesn't make it worthless. However, I don't play Beta much so I guess take that with a grain of salt.

Regarding the Human's economy... that's an intended limitation of their design. Interesting to note, Refineries can cross-map mine with no loss of productivity: they'll automatically produce Harvesters until the promised income rate is reached. This makes the Human limitation protecting their mining operations, not dealing with a lower income than the Beta or Goo. This is offset by generally more survivable units, an easier time tech switching than Beta have, and the best turrets in the game (though perhaps the new Shroud's turrets might be better, a little early to tell)

What you see as design flaws, I see as carefully considered design choices with subtle but important implications on gameplay. One of the most fascinating things about Grey Goo to me is how playing as a different faction COMPLETELY changes how you think about the map. Each faction's method of production and expansion is impacted by map design in different ways, and that's something Petroglyph has been experimenting with at least since Universe at War, perhaps this was true in Empire at War as well to an extent.

This expansion launch is a good opportunity for old players to come back and try new content, and for new players to get in with a lower cost of entry (to say nothing of 50% off sales being $15 now and 60% off sales being $10) I'm hoping that more people will come back to the game, and new people will give it a look thanks to the lower cost.

The new faction and new units for existing factions promise to add a lot of new dimensions to the game, which already had some surprising (imvho) depth under the surface for players who chose to look. The Beta and Goo factions, especially, had some research options that really changed how the factions were played, such as exploding Beta Commandos or Goo Devastators with bouncing attacks. I'm hopeful that with the Shroud, more people will try and stick with the game.

To be entirely fair, the different base building aspects of the various races actually are nothing new - as a matter of fact, Earth 2160 more or less had the exact same thing - large, sprawling bases with structures connected by tunnel/energy networks (Eurasian Dynasty/Humans), singular main structures onto which you add production add-ons (United Civilized States/ Beta), or no actual buildings but only special units that suck up resources so you can either clone or upgrade them into more advanced units (Aliens/Goo). And that years before Grey Goo came out.

As I've said, I've only played the game for a short while during a free weekend on Steam, though, so I perhaps simply don't have enough hours under the buckle to see the full use of certain units, such as the aforementioned Guardian. I just find it odd that there's a unit that can't do anything on its own - an "upgrade" for wall structures and the Hand of Ruk that spawns the guardians on board (kinda like interceptors for Starcraft's Carriers) would have seemed more sensible to me (although this, in turn, naturally would have led to issues when you want something other than guardians to man your stuff).

EDIT - I also never claimed that we've never seen this style of basebuilding before and don't really see how it's germane to the conversation at all. In fact, my previous post actually mentions Universe at War specifically, which ALSO saw variations on the general theme of "factions whose basebuilding dynamics impact how they approach the map". I think a comparison of Universe at War and Grey Goo could be interesting, as many of Grey Goo's design choices were influenced by balance issues caused by mechanics in Universe at War. Either way, it wouldn't surprise me if the Grey Goo dev team acknowledged both UAW and E2160 as inspirations, or at least that they had these games in mind when creating Grey Goo. I still don't really see how that's supposed to be a bad thing.

There are plenty of RTS with units with situational uses, I don't see this as surprising or unwarranted. Also, the Guardian's high DPS offsets this downside: once you cam mount it, it's one of the best DPS for cost in the game. It is weird though that you're fixated on this one unit as an example of what's wrong with the game. Especially after I pointed out that for Beta, offensive turreting is a viable and often-used strategy.

Yes, Earth 2160 did similar things, and I think that's fine. I really like seeing factions in an RTS have drastically different approaches to base design and construction (though the LC towers from that game, which you didn't mention, were very weird). Also, in my very humble opinion, Grey Goo manages to work out many of the kinks that were seen in Earth 2160s model. To me, at least, the UEF and Alien factions, the aliens in particular, were very unintuitive to work with. The Goo make it very clear how to expand, and the status of each Mother, and the options available for morphing Proteans into units, etc etc.

You also might look at the Zhon from TA: Kingdoms, who only had units that produced other units. They had builder units for T1 units, a different builder unit for T2 units, and ofc a different builder for T3 units.

What I like about Grey Goo that I don't remember as much from Earth 2160 is that each faction's building mechanic drastically changes how they approach terrain. A Goo player feels very differently about wide-spaced resource points than a Beta or Human player, and a Human player feels very differently about maps with lots of mountains than a Goo player. All factions, more or less, have tools at hand to deal with varying types of terrain, but they also approach each map in a unique way, which I very much enjoy. I don't think enough RTS focus on how the terrain of a map molds how their faction approaches or implements a successful strategy and I think that's very cool.

We also see in Grey Goo the upgrade system, which I don't think gets enough appreciation. Upgrades in Grey Goo aren't like, +1 damage or +1 armor, they actually substantially change how different unit types work in interesting ways. A timely upgrade to permanently stealth a unit type can (but won't necessarily) win games against unprepared opponents, there are upgrades that turn anti-armor units into anti-infantry, allowing the player to retool their army to better counter what their opponent is doing. Upgrades in Grey Goo are a very interesting system with, at least for the Beta and Goo (some Human upgrades I find to be a little underwhelming, which is frustrating as they're my favorite faction) the potential to really alter the player's approach to the game, and really influence what one's opponent has to do to deal with your army.

I don't expect to change your mind about the game. If you don't like it, that's all right: you gave it a try and it wasn't for you.

I did want to respond (and I hope I've done so respectfully) to provide an answer for any undecided person who might stumble across this conversation. I think Grey Goo is a worthwhile RTS to try, I feel like it has depth that might not be apparent at first glance. Especially after Descent of the Shroud, Grey Goo has many options for skillful play and for interesting counter-play. It has elements we've seen before in other places, sure, but I don't think that necessarily means anything bad: good ideas are good ideas. People didn't dislike Supreme Commander in its borrowing of ideas from Total Annihilation, nor did they dislike Planetary Annihilation for its own take on that model ( they disliked it for other reasons :p ).
